newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Strong quake kills at least 28 in Venezuela.
newsitem.headline: Strong quake kills at least 28 in Venezuela.

text.p: A powerful earthquake measuring 6.7 on the Richter scale rocked Venezuela's central and eastern coastal region on Wednesday, toppling buildings and killing at least 28 people, authorities said.
Office buildings and schools were flattened by the tremor -- Venezuela's worst for three decades -- and officials said the death toll could rise.

Mauricio Ruiz, information director of the eastern Sucre state said 22 people were killed in the small Caribbean coastal fishing town Cariaco and another six in the historic city Cumana, 255 miles (408 km) east of Caracas.
The deaths were caused by the collapse of a high school in Cariaco and a city center office building in Cumana, Ruiz told Reuters in a brief conversation by cellular telephone.
Telephone, water and power lines were downed, but there were no reports of fires, he said.
The insurance company tower block where at least six people lost their lives in Cumana "is totally wrecked and converted into a pile of metal and bricks," Ruiz said.
In addition to the deaths there were at least 82 people injured in Cariaco and Cumana, he said. Cariaco is about 35 miles (60 km) east of Cumana.

The quake, believed to be the worst to hit Venezuela since 1967, struck at about 3:25 p.m. (1925 GMT) and measured 6.7 on the open-ended Richter scale, FUNVISIS seismological institute officials in Caracas said.
FUNVISIS officials had earlier measured the quake at only about 5.5 on the Richter scale, although the U.S. Geological Survey in Golden, Colorado said it measured 6.9.
The epicenter was about 30 miles (49 km) off Venezuela's northeastern Caribbean coast and there were five aftershocks, the last at 5:40 p.m. (2140 GMT), they said.

Despite the size of the quake, state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela said both production and export continued to flow smoothly. Venezuela is the largest exporter of gasoline to the United States.
In Cumana, rescue workers worked into the night to find survivors in the rubble of the collapsed tower block, which crumbled when the first tremor hit.
"There are several bodies inside the building but we are working to remove them later because those who are alive are the priority," fireman Fernando Ramirez told Radio Caracas Radio.
Ramirez said the death toll from the office building collapse could rise "because according to our information 60 to 70 people worked in the building."
A Cumana resident who spoke to Reuters by cellular phone said the building had folded in on itself. "It just collapsed," he said.
A school in Cumana also collapsed but there was nobody in it at the time, Ramirez said.

In Cariaco, preliminary reports said 22 people were killed when a high school collapsed in the quake, which occurred during school hours. There were no other details immediately available, but reports said one other school and another building also collapsed in the town, where telephone lines were down.
Founded in 1521, Cumana is the oldest inhabited city in South America. However most of its colonial architecture was destroyed in a massive earthquake in 1797.
The 1967 quake, the last to cause serious damage in Venezuela, killed 215 people in the capital and surrounding area, FUNVISIS officials said.
State Governor Ramon Martinez declared a state of emergency and told residents in Cumana to assemble at local sports fields.

On the nearby island of Margarita, just off Venezuela's northeastern coastline, officials said the airport was closed and power cut off after an undersea electricity cable linking the island with Cumana was damaged. The quake also caused the collapse of Margarita's Customs House, which fell on top of about 60 cars.
